1-1.title: Complete Sentences vs. Fragments
1-1.learn:
HOW TO TELL A COMPLETE SENTENCE FROM A FRAGMENT

A complete sentence needs THREE things: a subject (who or what), a verb (the action or state of being), and a complete thought. If even one is missing, it is a fragment.

Example 1 — 'The dog barked loudly.'
Step 1: Find the subject. WHO or WHAT? 'The dog.'
Step 2: Find the verb. What did it do? 'barked.'
Step 3: Is it a full thought? Yes — you know who did what.
Result: This is a COMPLETE sentence.

Example 2 — 'Barking loudly in the yard.'
Step 1: Find the verb-like word: 'Barking.'
Step 2: Find the subject. WHO is barking? It never says!
Result: No subject = a FRAGMENT. Fix it: 'The dog was barking loudly in the yard.'

Example 3 — 'Because I finished my homework.'
Step 1: Subject = 'I,' verb = 'finished.'
Step 2: But it starts with 'Because,' which leaves you waiting. Then what?
Result: It is not a complete thought, so it is a FRAGMENT. Fix it: 'Because I finished my homework, I watched TV.'

questions.question: Which of these is a COMPLETE sentence?

choices.A: Running down the street.
choices.B: The runner crossed the finish line.
choices.C: When the bell rang.

questions.explanation: It has a subject ('The runner'), a verb ('crossed'), and a complete thought. The others are missing a subject, a verb, or a full idea.

questions.question: Which of these is a FRAGMENT?

choices.A: The cat slept on the couch.
choices.B: Birds sang in the trees.
choices.C: Standing quietly by the door.

questions.explanation: 'Standing quietly by the door' has no subject — we never learn WHO is standing — so it is a fragment.

choices.B: A verb

questions.explanation: It names a subject (the player) but never says what he did or is, so it is missing a verb.

choices.B: While skating across the ice.
choices.C: Maria was skating across the ice.

questions.explanation: Adding the subject 'Maria' and the verb 'was' creates a complete thought. The others still lack a subject or a finished idea.

choices.B: The crowd cheered.

choices.A: It has no verb.
choices.B: It has no subject.
choices.C: It starts with 'Although' and never finishes the thought.

choices.C: It has too many adjectives; remove some words.

1-2.title: Independent & Dependent Clauses
1-2.learn:
HOW TO TELL INDEPENDENT FROM DEPENDENT CLAUSES

A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. An INDEPENDENT clause expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence. A DEPENDENT clause has a subject and verb too, but it starts with a word like 'because,' 'when,' 'although,' 'since,' or 'if,' so it CANNOT stand alone.

Example 1 — 'I finished my homework.'
Step 1: Subject = 'I,' verb = 'finished.'
Step 2: Does it stand alone and feel complete? Yes.
Result: INDEPENDENT clause.

Example 2 — 'Because I finished my homework.'
Step 1: Same subject and verb, but it begins with 'Because.'
Step 2: It leaves you hanging — then what happened?
Result: DEPENDENT clause. It needs an independent clause to be complete.

Example 3 — Joining them: 'Because I finished my homework, I watched TV.'
Step 1: The dependent clause ('Because I finished my homework') sets up the idea.
Step 2: The independent clause ('I watched TV') completes it.
Result: A complete sentence. Words like because, when, although, since, if, while signal a DEPENDENT clause.

questions.question: Which group of words is an INDEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: When the bell rang
choices.B: Because it was late
choices.C: Although she tried hard

questions.explanation: 'The students left the room' has a subject and verb and stands alone as a complete thought. The others begin with words that make them dependent.

questions.question: Which group of words is a DEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: The rain stopped
choices.B: We ate lunch outside
choices.C: Since the sun came out

questions.explanation: 'Since the sun came out' starts with 'Since,' which makes it dependent — it cannot stand alone.

questions.question: Which word at the start of a clause makes it DEPENDENT?

choices.A: The
choices.B: Although
choices.C: Quickly

questions.explanation: 'Although' is a subordinating word that begins a dependent clause and leaves the thought unfinished.

questions.question: In 'When the movie ended, we walked home,' which part is the DEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: When the movie ended
choices.B: we walked home
choices.C: the movie

questions.explanation: 'When the movie ended' begins with 'When' and cannot stand alone, so it is the dependent clause.

questions.question: In 'If you study, you will pass,' which part is the INDEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: If you study
choices.B: you will pass
choices.C: If you

questions.explanation: 'You will pass' stands alone as a complete thought, while 'If you study' is dependent.

questions.question: Which sentence is made of TWO independent clauses joined together?

choices.A: Because she was tired, she rested.
choices.B: The dog barked, and the cat ran away.
choices.C: When the bus arrived, we boarded.

questions.explanation: Both 'The dog barked' and 'the cat ran away' can stand alone, so they are two independent clauses joined by 'and.'

questions.question: Which choice is a complete sentence rather than just a dependent clause?

choices.A: While I waited for the train.
choices.B: Since the store was closed.
choices.C: The team practiced all morning.

questions.explanation: 'The team practiced all morning' is independent and complete; the others are dependent clauses left hanging.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly joins a dependent and an independent clause?

choices.A: Although I was nervous, I gave the speech.
choices.B: Although I was nervous I gave the speech.
choices.C: Although I was nervous.

questions.explanation: When a dependent clause comes first, a comma separates it from the independent clause: 'Although I was nervous, I gave the speech.'

questions.question: Why can't 'Whenever the alarm goes off in the morning' be a sentence by itself?

choices.A: It has no subject.
choices.B: It has no verb.
choices.C: It starts with 'Whenever,' which makes it dependent and leaves the thought unfinished.

questions.explanation: It has a subject ('the alarm') and verb ('goes off'), but 'Whenever' makes it dependent, so the thought is incomplete.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a dependent clause AFTER the independent clause?

choices.A: Because the road was icy, we drove slowly.
choices.B: We drove slowly because the road was icy.
choices.C: The road was icy, and we drove slowly.

questions.explanation: In choice B, the independent clause 'We drove slowly' comes first, followed by the dependent clause 'because the road was icy.'

questions.question: Which group of words is an INDEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: Although the test was hard
choices.B: When the lights dimmed
choices.C: The audience cheered

questions.explanation: 'The audience cheered' has a subject and a verb and stands alone as a complete thought; the others begin with words that make them dependent.

questions.question: Which group of words is a DEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: The phone rang
choices.B: She answered quickly
choices.C: Before the show started

questions.explanation: 'Before the show started' begins with 'Before,' which makes it dependent — it cannot stand alone.

questions.question: Which word at the start of a clause makes it DEPENDENT?

choices.A: Because
choices.B: The
choices.C: Slowly

questions.explanation: 'Because' is a subordinating word that begins a dependent clause and leaves the thought unfinished.

questions.question: Which group of words is an INDEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: Since it was raining
choices.B: If you ask politely
choices.C: While the kettle boiled

questions.explanation: 'The garden needed water' stands alone as a complete thought; the others start with subordinating words.

questions.question: Which group of words is a DEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: The team scored
choices.B: Although they were losing
choices.C: Fans waved flags

questions.explanation: 'Although they were losing' begins with 'Although,' making it dependent — it needs more to be complete.

questions.question: Which word could start a DEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: When
choices.B: Happily
choices.C: Quickly

questions.explanation: 'When' is a subordinating word that begins a dependent clause; the others are adverbs that do not make a clause dependent.

questions.question: Which choice is a complete sentence rather than just a dependent clause?

choices.A: Since the library was quiet.
choices.B: After the rain finally stopped.
choices.C: The volunteers planted new trees.

questions.explanation: 'The volunteers planted new trees' is independent and complete; the others are dependent clauses left hanging.

questions.question: Which group of words is an INDEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: Whenever the alarm rings
choices.B: If the alarm rings
choices.C: Until the alarm rings

questions.explanation: 'My alarm rings at six' stands alone as a complete thought; the others begin with subordinating words.

questions.question: Which group of words is a DEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: We packed our bags
choices.B: The plane took off
choices.C: Until the storm passed

questions.explanation: 'Until the storm passed' starts with 'Until,' which makes it dependent and unable to stand alone.

questions.question: Which group of words is an INDEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: As the sun rose slowly
choices.B: Though we were tired
choices.C: We packed the car early

questions.explanation: 'We packed the car early' is a complete thought that can stand alone; the others are dependent clauses.

questions.question: In 'After the storm passed, the birds returned,' which part is the DEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: After the storm passed
choices.B: the birds returned
choices.C: the storm

questions.explanation: 'After the storm passed' begins with 'After' and cannot stand alone, so it is the dependent clause.

questions.question: In 'Since you are ready, we can leave now,' which part is the INDEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: Since you are ready
choices.B: we can leave now
choices.C: Since you

questions.explanation: 'We can leave now' stands alone as a complete thought, while 'Since you are ready' is dependent.

questions.question: Which sentence is made of TWO independent clauses joined together?

choices.B: Although it was cold, we swam.
choices.C: Because she was kind, everyone liked her.
choices.D: The sky cleared, and the sun came out.

questions.explanation: Both 'The sky cleared' and 'the sun came out' can stand alone, so they are two independent clauses joined by 'and.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly joins a dependent and an independent clause?

choices.A: Because I was hungry, I made a sandwich.
choices.B: Because I was hungry I made a sandwich.
choices.C: Because I was hungry.

questions.explanation: When a dependent clause comes first, a comma separates it from the independent clause: 'Because I was hungry, I made a sandwich.'

questions.question: In 'While the soup simmered, we set the table,' which part is the DEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: we set the table
choices.B: While the soup simmered
choices.C: the soup

questions.explanation: 'While the soup simmered' begins with 'While' and cannot stand alone, so it is the dependent clause.

questions.question: Which choice is a complete sentence rather than just a dependent clause?

choices.A: After the long flight to Miami.
choices.B: Because the meeting ran late.
choices.C: The chef prepared a special dessert.
choices.D: While the band tuned their instruments.

questions.explanation: 'The chef prepared a special dessert' is independent and complete; the others are dependent clauses left unfinished.

questions.question: In 'If we leave now, we will beat the traffic,' which part is the INDEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: If we leave now
choices.B: leave now
choices.C: If we

questions.explanation: 'We will beat the traffic' is a complete thought that stands alone; 'If we leave now' is dependent.

choices.B: When the rain stopped, we went outside.

choices.B: Although the movie was long, we stayed.
choices.C: When the movie ended, we left.
choices.D: Because the movie was scary, I hid.

questions.explanation: Both 'The movie ended' and 'we drove home' can stand alone, so they are two independent clauses joined by 'and.'

questions.question: In 'We canceled the picnic because a storm was coming,' which part is the DEPENDENT clause?

choices.A: We canceled the picnic
choices.B: because a storm was coming
choices.C: a storm

questions.explanation: 'Because a storm was coming' starts with 'because' and cannot stand alone, so it is the dependent clause, even though it comes second.

questions.question: Why can't 'Although the museum was crowded that afternoon' be a sentence by itself?

choices.A: It has no subject.
choices.B: It has no verb.
choices.C: It starts with 'Although,' which makes it dependent and leaves the thought unfinished.

questions.explanation: It has a subject ('the museum') and a verb ('was'), but 'Although' makes it dependent, so the thought is incomplete.

choices.B: The game was delayed because the field was muddy.
choices.C: The field was muddy, and the game was delayed.

1-3.title: Run-On Sentences & Comma Splices
1-3.learn:
HOW TO SPOT AND FIX RUN-ONS AND COMMA SPLICES

A RUN-ON jams two complete sentences together with no punctuation: 'I love pizza I eat it daily.' A COMMA SPLICE glues two complete sentences with only a comma: 'I love pizza, I eat it daily.' Both are errors.

Three ways to fix them:
1) Use a period: 'I love pizza. I eat it daily.'
2) Use a semicolon: 'I love pizza; I eat it daily.'
3) Use a comma PLUS a joining word (and, but, so, or): 'I love pizza, and I eat it daily.'

Example 1 — 'The bell rang we left class.'
This is a run-on (no punctuation between two sentences). Fix: 'The bell rang, and we left class.'

Example 2 — 'It was cold, we wore coats.'
This is a comma splice (only a comma between two sentences). Fix: 'It was cold, so we wore coats.'

Example 3 — Test it: cover everything before the comma. If what's left is a full sentence AND what's before it is too, you need more than a comma.

1-4.title: Simple, Compound & Complex Sentences
1-4.learn:
HOW TO IDENTIFY SIMPLE, COMPOUND, AND COMPLEX SENTENCES

SIMPLE = one independent clause (one complete thought): 'Rain fell.'
COMPOUND = two independent clauses joined by a comma + FANBOYS (and, but, or, so, etc.) or a semicolon: 'Rain fell, and the game stopped.'
COMPLEX = one independent clause + at least one dependent clause (starts with because, when, although, etc.): 'When rain fell, the game stopped.'

Example 1 — 'The bell rang.'
One complete thought, no joining words. Type: SIMPLE.

Example 2 — 'The bell rang, and students rushed out.'
Two complete thoughts joined by comma + 'and.' Type: COMPOUND.

Example 3 — 'When the bell rang, students rushed out.'
'When the bell rang' is dependent; 'students rushed out' is independent. Type: COMPLEX.

Quick check: Count the complete-thought parts. One part = simple. Two equal parts joined = compound. One part that needs the other (starts with because/when/if) = complex.

questions.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by comma + 'but' make this compound; A and D are complex and C is simple.

questions.question: What type of sentence is 'The fireworks exploded; the children cheered'?

choices.A: Simple
choices.B: Compound
choices.C: Complex

questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, which makes it a compound sentence.

questions.question: Which sentence combines ideas into a COMPLEX sentence correctly?

choices.A: He laughed and he clapped.
choices.B: He laughed. He clapped.
choices.C: Because the joke was funny, he laughed and clapped.

questions.explanation: Adding the dependent clause 'Because the joke was funny' to an independent clause creates a complex sentence.

questions.question: Identify the sentence type: 'Since the test was tomorrow, I studied all evening.'

choices.A: Simple, one clause
choices.B: Compound, two independent clauses
choices.C: Complex, a dependent clause plus an independent clause

questions.explanation: 'Since the test was tomorrow' is dependent and 'I studied all evening' is independent, so the sentence is complex.

questions.question: What type of sentence is 'The dancers practiced for weeks, and their show was a hit'?

choices.A: Simple
choices.B: Compound
choices.C: Complex

questions.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by a comma plus 'and,' so it is a compound sentence.

questions.question: Which sentence is SIMPLE, even though it looks complicated?

choices.A: After the long winter, the bright flowers bloomed across the entire valley.
choices.B: The flowers bloomed, and the bees buzzed.
choices.C: When the flowers bloomed, the bees buzzed.
choices.D: The flowers bloomed; the bees buzzed.

questions.explanation: Choice A has one independent clause with introductory phrases, so it is simple. The others contain two clauses.

questions.question: Which sentence is the ONLY COMPLEX sentence?

choices.A: The bus arrived, and we boarded.
choices.B: The bus arrived on time.
choices.C: When the bus arrived, we boarded quickly.

questions.explanation: Only choice C joins a dependent clause ('When the bus arrived') with an independent clause, making it complex.

questions.question: Identify the sentence type: 'The storm passed, and the sun returned.'

choices.A: Simple, one clause
choices.B: Compound, two independent clauses joined by a comma and 'and'
choices.C: Complex, a dependent clause plus an independent clause

questions.explanation: Both 'The storm passed' and 'the sun returned' are independent, joined by a comma plus 'and,' so it is compound.

questions.question: Which sentence is the ONLY SIMPLE sentence?

choices.A: The scientist mixed the chemicals carefully in the lab.
choices.B: The scientist mixed the chemicals, and the mixture bubbled.
choices.C: When the scientist mixed the chemicals, the mixture bubbled.
choices.D: The scientist mixed the chemicals; the mixture bubbled.

questions.explanation: Only choice A has a single independent clause. The others contain two clauses (compound or complex).

questions.question: What type of sentence is 'Whenever it rains, the streets near the school flood quickly'?

choices.A: Simple
choices.B: Compound
choices.C: Complex

questions.explanation: 'Whenever it rains' is a dependent clause joined to the independent clause 'the streets near the school flood quickly,' so it is complex.

questions.question: Which sentence is COMPOUND, not complex?

choices.A: Because the alarm sounded, everyone left the building.
choices.B: When the alarm sounded, everyone left the building.
choices.C: The alarm sounded, so everyone left the building.
choices.D: Everyone left the building after the alarm sounded.

questions.explanation: Choice C joins two independent clauses with a comma plus 'so,' making it compound. The others use subordinating words and are complex.

1-5.title: Varying Sentence Structure
1-5.learn:
HOW TO VARY SENTENCE STRUCTURE

Good writing mixes short and long sentences and starts them in different ways. When every sentence is the same length and starts with the subject, writing sounds choppy and robotic.

Example 1 — Choppy: 'I ran. I was tired. I stopped.'
These are three short, identical sentences. Combine and vary them: 'Exhausted, I finally stopped running.' Now one smooth sentence replaces three choppy ones.

Example 2 — Repetitive starts: 'The dog barked. The dog ran. The dog jumped.'
Every sentence starts with 'The dog.' Vary the openings: 'Barking loudly, the dog ran across the yard and jumped the fence.'

Example 3 — Mixing lengths for effect: 'The night was quiet. Then, without warning, a loud crash echoed through the empty house and made everyone freeze.'
A short sentence followed by a long one builds interest. To vary sentences: change their length, change how they start (with a describing word, a phrase, or a dependent clause), and combine choppy ones.

questions.question: Which revision BEST varies these choppy sentences: 'I was scared. I kept walking. I reached the door.'?

choices.A: Although I was scared, I kept walking until I reached the door.
choices.B: I was scared. I kept walking. I reached the door.
choices.C: I was scared and I was scared and I reached the door.

questions.explanation: Choice A combines the choppy sentences into one smooth, varied sentence with a dependent-clause opener.

questions.question: What is the main problem with writing that uses only short sentences of the same length?

choices.A: It sounds choppy and robotic.
choices.B: It has too many commas.
choices.C: It always has spelling errors.
choices.D: It uses too many big words.

questions.explanation: Many short, identical sentences in a row make writing sound choppy and dull instead of smooth.

questions.question: Which sentence starts with something OTHER than the subject for variety?

choices.A: The team won the championship.
choices.B: After a long season, the team won the championship.
choices.C: The team practiced every day.

questions.explanation: Choice B begins with the introductory phrase 'After a long season' instead of the subject, adding variety.

questions.question: Which paragraph shows the BEST sentence variety?

choices.A: I like books. I read often. I have many.
choices.B: Books books books. I read read read.
choices.C: I love to read. Whenever I have free time, I curl up with a good book and lose track of the hours.
choices.D: I like books and I read often and I have many books and I read them.

questions.explanation: Choice C mixes a short sentence with a longer, differently structured one, showing strong variety.

questions.question: Which revision combines 'The wind blew. Leaves fell. The sky darkened.' into one varied sentence?

choices.A: The wind blew and leaves fell and the sky darkened.
choices.B: The wind blew. Leaves fell. The sky darkened.
choices.C: Wind, leaves, sky.
choices.D: As the wind blew, leaves fell and the sky darkened.

questions.explanation: Choice D uses a dependent clause opener and combines the ideas smoothly, varying the structure.

questions.question: Which sentence opening adds variety by starting with a describing word (an -ed or -ing word)?

choices.A: The runner crossed the line.
choices.B: Exhausted, the runner crossed the line.
choices.C: The runner was very tired at the line.
choices.D: The runner slowly crossed the line.

questions.explanation: Starting with the participle 'Exhausted' varies the opening instead of beginning with the subject.

questions.question: Why might a writer follow a long sentence with a very short one?

choices.A: To create emphasis or a dramatic effect.
choices.B: Because short sentences are always wrong.
choices.C: To use up extra words.
choices.D: Because long sentences are not allowed.

questions.explanation: Mixing a long sentence with a short, punchy one creates emphasis and keeps readers interested.

questions.question: Which choice fixes the repetitive openings in 'She opened the box. She found a note. She smiled.'?

choices.A: She opened the box. She found a note. She smiled.
choices.B: She, she, she opened, found, smiled.
choices.C: Opening the box, she found a note and smiled.
choices.D: She opened and she found and she smiled the box note.

questions.explanation: Choice C combines the three sentences and varies the opening with a participial phrase, removing the repeated 'She.'

questions.question: Which revision improves variety the MOST without losing meaning: 'The storm came. The power went out. We lit candles. We waited.'?

choices.A: The storm came, the power went out, we lit candles, we waited.
choices.B: The storm came. The power went out. We lit candles. We waited.
choices.C: When the storm came and the power went out, we lit candles and waited.

questions.explanation: Choice C combines the choppy sentences using a dependent clause and 'and,' creating smooth, varied structure.

questions.question: A writer's draft reads: 'The hike was hard. The hike was long. The hike was worth it.' What is the BEST single revision?

choices.A: The hike was hard. The hike was long. The hike was worth it.
choices.B: Hard and long, the hike was worth it.
choices.C: The hike was hard and long and worth it and hard.

questions.explanation: Choice B combines the repetitive sentences into one varied sentence that opens with describing words and keeps the meaning.

questions.question: Which revision BEST varies these choppy sentences: 'The dog ran. The dog jumped. The dog barked.'?

choices.A: The dog ran, jumped, and barked happily in the yard.
choices.B: The dog ran. The dog jumped. The dog barked.
choices.C: The dog ran and the dog jumped and the dog barked.

questions.explanation: Choice A combines the three choppy sentences into one smooth sentence and removes the repeated 'The dog.'

questions.question: What is the main problem with starting every sentence with the same subject, like 'I'?

choices.A: It makes the writing sound repetitive and dull.
choices.B: It always creates run-on sentences.
choices.C: It removes all the verbs.

questions.explanation: Beginning every sentence the same way makes writing sound repetitive and boring instead of smooth and interesting.

questions.question: Which sentence starts with something OTHER than the subject for variety?

choices.A: We watched the parade downtown.
choices.B: We cheered for the floats.
choices.C: We waved our flags.
choices.D: Early in the morning, we watched the parade downtown.

questions.explanation: Choice D begins with the introductory phrase 'Early in the morning' instead of the subject, adding variety.

questions.question: Which choice shows the BEST sentence variety?

choices.A: I have a cat. I have a dog. I have a fish.
choices.B: Cat dog fish. I have. I have.
choices.C: I love animals. My house is home to a playful cat, a loyal dog, and a quiet goldfish.
choices.D: I have a cat and I have a dog and I have a fish and I love them.

questions.explanation: Choice C mixes a short sentence with a longer, differently structured one, showing strong variety.

questions.question: Which sentence opening adds variety by starting with an -ing word?

choices.A: The swimmer dove into the pool.
choices.B: The swimmer made a big splash today.
choices.C: The swimmer was quick in the pool.
choices.D: Diving into the pool, the swimmer made a splash.

questions.explanation: Starting with the -ing word 'Diving' varies the opening instead of beginning with the subject.

questions.question: Why do good writers mix short and long sentences?

choices.A: To keep writing interesting and to control the rhythm.
choices.B: Because short sentences are always wrong.
choices.C: To make the writing harder to read.
choices.D: Because long sentences are not allowed.

questions.explanation: Mixing sentence lengths keeps the rhythm interesting and prevents writing from sounding choppy or dull.

questions.question: Which sentence opening starts with a dependent clause for variety?

choices.A: We stayed inside all day.
choices.B: Because the rain never stopped, we stayed inside all day.
choices.C: We watched movies all day.
choices.D: We made popcorn and watched movies.

questions.explanation: Choice B opens with the dependent clause 'Because the rain never stopped' instead of the subject, adding variety.

questions.question: Which revision varies these choppy sentences: 'The car stopped. The door opened. A man stepped out.'?

choices.A: When the car stopped, the door opened and a man stepped out.
choices.B: The car stopped. The door opened. A man stepped out.
choices.C: Car door man. Stopped opened stepped.
choices.D: The car stopped and the door opened and a man stepped out and waited.

questions.explanation: Choice A combines the three short sentences using a dependent clause opener, creating smooth variety.

questions.question: Which sentence begins with a describing word instead of the subject?

choices.A: The hikers reached the summit at noon.
choices.B: The hikers were tired at the summit.
choices.C: Exhausted but proud, the hikers reached the summit at noon.
choices.D: The hikers slowly reached the summit.

questions.explanation: Choice C opens with the describing words 'Exhausted but proud' instead of starting with the subject, adding variety.

questions.question: Which choice fixes the repetitive openings in 'He grabbed his bag. He ran outside. He caught the bus.'?

choices.A: He grabbed his bag. He ran outside. He caught the bus.
choices.B: Grabbing his bag, he ran outside and caught the bus.
choices.C: He, he, he grabbed ran caught.
choices.D: He grabbed and he ran and he caught the bag bus outside.

questions.explanation: Choice B combines the sentences and varies the opening with an -ing phrase, removing the repeated 'He.'

questions.question: Which revision BEST combines 'The crowd grew quiet. The speaker stepped up. The speech began.' into one varied sentence?

choices.A: The crowd grew quiet and the speaker stepped up and the speech began.
choices.B: The crowd grew quiet. The speaker stepped up. The speech began.
choices.C: As the crowd grew quiet, the speaker stepped up and began the speech.

questions.explanation: Choice C uses a dependent-clause opener and combines the ideas smoothly, varying the structure.

questions.question: Which paragraph shows the BEST sentence variety?

choices.A: Soccer is fun. I play soccer. I like soccer.
choices.B: I play soccer every Saturday. After a hard week, nothing feels better than running across the green field with my friends.
choices.C: Soccer soccer soccer. Play play play.
choices.D: I play soccer and I like soccer and soccer is fun and I play it.

questions.explanation: Choice B mixes a short sentence with a longer, differently structured one, creating strong variety.

questions.question: Which sentence starts with a prepositional phrase to add variety?

choices.A: The keys were under the couch cushions.
choices.B: The keys were lost for an hour.
choices.C: The keys were silver and shiny.
choices.D: Under the couch cushions, the keys were finally found.

questions.explanation: Choice D opens with the prepositional phrase 'Under the couch cushions' instead of the subject, adding variety.

questions.question: Which revision improves variety the MOST: 'The alarm rang. I jumped up. I got dressed. I rushed out.'?

choices.A: The alarm rang, I jumped up, I got dressed, I rushed out.
choices.B: When the alarm rang, I jumped up, got dressed, and rushed out.
choices.C: The alarm rang. I jumped up. I got dressed. I rushed out.

questions.explanation: Choice B opens with a dependent clause and combines the choppy sentences smoothly without losing meaning.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a participial (-ing) opener for variety?

choices.A: The chef tasted the soup and added salt.
choices.B: The chef quickly added salt to the soup.
choices.C: Tasting the soup, the chef added a pinch of salt.
choices.D: The chef added salt because the soup was bland.

questions.explanation: Choice C begins with the participial phrase 'Tasting the soup' instead of the subject, varying the opening.

questions.question: Why might a writer use a very short sentence after several long ones?

choices.A: To create emphasis and grab the reader's attention.
choices.B: Because long sentences are always wrong.
choices.C: To confuse the reader on purpose.
choices.D: Because short sentences cannot have verbs.

questions.explanation: A short, punchy sentence after longer ones creates emphasis and draws the reader's attention.

questions.question: Which revision best combines 'It was getting dark. We packed our gear. We headed home.'?

choices.A: It was getting dark we packed our gear we headed home.
choices.B: Because it was getting dark, we packed our gear and headed home.
choices.C: It was getting dark. We packed our gear. We headed home.

questions.explanation: Choice B opens with a dependent clause and joins the remaining ideas, creating smooth, varied structure.

questions.question: Which choice fixes the repetitive structure in 'The movie was exciting. The movie was funny. The movie was long.'?

choices.A: The movie was exciting. The movie was funny. The movie was long.
choices.B: Exciting, funny, and a little long, the movie kept us entertained.
choices.C: The movie was exciting funny long.
choices.D: Movie exciting movie funny movie long.

questions.explanation: Choice B combines the repeated sentences into one varied sentence that opens with describing words and keeps the meaning.

questions.question: Which sentence adds variety by opening with a transition word?

choices.A: We lost the first game. We won the next two.
choices.B: We won the next two games easily.
choices.C: We played hard in every game.
choices.D: However, we bounced back and won the next two games.

questions.explanation: Choice D begins with the transition word 'However,' which varies the opening and links ideas smoothly.

questions.question: Which revision combines 'The wind picked up. The kite soared. The children laughed.' into one varied sentence?

choices.A: The wind picked up and the kite soared and the children laughed.
choices.B: As the wind picked up, the kite soared and the children laughed.
choices.C: The wind picked up. The kite soared. The children laughed.

questions.explanation: Choice B uses a dependent-clause opener ('As the wind picked up') and combines the ideas smoothly, varying the structure.

questions.question: Which revision improves variety the MOST without losing meaning: 'The bell rang. Students grabbed their bags. They poured into the hallway. The school day ended.'?

choices.A: The bell rang, students grabbed their bags, they poured into the hallway, the school day ended.
choices.B: The bell rang. Students grabbed their bags. They poured into the hallway. The school day ended.
choices.C: When the bell rang, students grabbed their bags and poured into the hallway, and the school day ended.

questions.explanation: Choice C combines the choppy sentences using a dependent clause and joining words, creating smooth, varied structure.

questions.question: A writer's draft reads: 'The room was dark. The room was cold. The room was silent.' What is the BEST single revision?

choices.A: The room was dark. The room was cold. The room was silent.
choices.B: The room was dark and cold and silent and dark.
choices.C: Room dark cold silent.
choices.D: Dark, cold, and silent, the room felt empty.

questions.explanation: Choice D combines the repetitive sentences into one varied sentence that opens with describing words and keeps the meaning.

questions.question: Which choice fixes the repetitive openings in 'She picked up the brush. She dipped it in paint. She painted the sky.'?

choices.A: She picked up the brush. She dipped it in paint. She painted the sky.
choices.B: She, she, she picked dipped painted.
choices.C: Picking up the brush and dipping it in paint, she painted the sky.
choices.D: She picked and she dipped and she painted brush paint sky.

questions.explanation: Choice C combines the three sentences and varies the opening with participial phrases, removing the repeated 'She.'

questions.question: Which paragraph uses the STRONGEST variety in both length and sentence openings?

choices.A: The team trained hard. The team won. The team celebrated.
choices.B: After months of grueling practice, the team finally won the championship. They celebrated all night. The trophy gleamed.
choices.C: The team trained and won and celebrated and trained again.
choices.D: Train win celebrate. Team team team.

questions.explanation: Choice B mixes a long opener, a medium sentence, and a short sentence, and it varies how sentences begin — the strongest variety.

questions.question: Which revision improves variety the MOST: 'The volcano rumbled. Smoke rose. People fled. The town emptied.'?

choices.A: The volcano rumbled, smoke rose, people fled, the town emptied.
choices.B: As the volcano rumbled and smoke rose, people fled until the town emptied.
choices.C: The volcano rumbled. Smoke rose. People fled. The town emptied.

questions.explanation: Choice B combines the choppy sentences with a dependent clause and 'until,' creating smooth, varied structure.

questions.question: A draft reads: 'I opened the letter. My hands shook. The news was good.' Which revision keeps the meaning but varies the sentences BEST?

choices.A: I opened the letter my hands shook the news was good.
choices.B: With shaking hands, I opened the letter — the news was good.
choices.C: I opened the letter and my hands shook and the news was good.

questions.explanation: Choice B opens with a phrase and uses a dash for emphasis, varying both the opening and the rhythm while keeping the meaning.

questions.question: Which revision shows variety by following a LONG sentence with a SHORT one for effect?

choices.A: The detective searched every room. The detective checked every drawer. The detective found nothing.
choices.B: The detective searched every room and checked every drawer, examining each corner with care. She found nothing.
choices.C: Detective searched checked found nothing.
choices.D: The detective searched and checked and found and searched again.

questions.explanation: Choice B pairs a long, detailed sentence with a short, punchy one ('She found nothing'), creating variety and emphasis.

questions.question: Which choice best fixes BOTH the repeated openings and the choppy length in 'The storm hit. The lights went out. We grabbed flashlights. We waited it out.'?

choices.A: The storm hit, the lights went out, we grabbed flashlights, we waited it out.
choices.B: When the storm hit and the lights went out, we grabbed flashlights and waited it out.
choices.C: The storm hit. The lights went out. We grabbed flashlights. We waited it out.

questions.explanation: Choice B opens with a dependent clause and combines the four choppy sentences smoothly, fixing both the repetition and the choppiness.

questions.question: A writer wants to vary this draft: 'The cake looked perfect. The cake smelled amazing. The cake tasted even better.' Which single revision is BEST?

choices.A: The cake looked perfect. The cake smelled amazing. The cake tasted even better.
choices.B: Perfect to look at and amazing to smell, the cake tasted even better.
choices.C: The cake looked and smelled and tasted perfect amazing better.

questions.explanation: Choice B combines the three repetitive sentences into one varied sentence with a descriptive opener while keeping the meaning.

questions.question: Which revision improves a choppy paragraph by varying sentence beginnings the MOST: 'The runners lined up. The gun fired. The runners sprinted. The crowd roared.'?

choices.A: The runners lined up, the gun fired, the runners sprinted, the crowd roared.
choices.B: The runners lined up. The gun fired. The runners sprinted. The crowd roared.
choices.C: As the runners lined up, the gun fired; instantly, they sprinted while the crowd roared.

questions.explanation: Choice C varies the openings with a dependent clause and a transition word and combines the choppy sentences smoothly.
